title: CAN CHRISTIANS SPEAK BIBLICALLY ABOUT SEXUAL SIN WITHOUT BECOMING SELF-RIGHTEOUS?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS SPEAK BIBLICALLY ABOUT SEXUAL SIN WITHOUT BECOMING SELF-RIGHTEOUS?

Yes. But only when the person speaking remembers that the ground beneath the sinner and the ground beneath the preacher is the same ground—and the only reason either can stand before God is Jesus Christ.
There is a dangerous moment that happens when Christians start talking about sexual sin.
It happens so quietly that sometimes we do not notice it.
We open the Bible.
We find the verse.
We identify the sin.
We explain what God condemns.
And somewhere between opening Scripture and closing the conversation, we forget something terrifyingly important:
We needed the Cross too.
Maybe your particular scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody found the messages.
Maybe nobody knows what you watched when the door was locked.
Maybe your marriage survived what almost destroyed it.
Maybe your struggle was pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe fornication.
Maybe lust.
Maybe same-sex sexual behavior.
Maybe secret fantasies.
Maybe an emotional affair you kept calling “friendship.”
Maybe you have never committed the sexual sins you condemn at all.
But perhaps pride found another door.
Perhaps bitterness did.
Perhaps greed.
Perhaps envy.
Perhaps gossip.
Perhaps you learned how to stand outside someone else's wreckage holding a Bible while forgetting the wreckage from which Jesus rescued you.
And that may be one of the most frightening forms of spiritual blindness:
being correct about somebody else's sin while becoming blind to your own need for grace.
So we need to ask the question Christians cannot afford to avoid:
Can we speak clearly, courageously, unapologetically, biblically about sexual sin without becoming self-righteous?
Yes.
We must.
But the answer is not to make sin smaller.
The answer is to make the Cross bigger.
Because Christianity does not force us to choose between truth and compassion.
At the Cross, we discover both.
Sexual sin is real.
God's holiness is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
And grace is breathtakingly real.

Paul did not soften Scripture when he wrote to Corinth. He named sexual immorality among sins incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom. But notice something people often miss when they weaponize this passage: Paul does not create a special category containing only sexual sinners.
His list also confronts idolaters, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers, and swindlers.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the New Testament.
The Greek says:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε· ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε…”
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified…”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Look carefully at those words.
Such were some of you.
Were.
Not because Corinth had discovered better public relations.
Not because Christians had learned how to hide their past.
Not because they had become morally superior to everybody outside the church.
Jesus had intervened.
They were washed.
They were sanctified.
They were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for avoiding the sins of bad people.
Dead people being made alive.
Guilty people being justified.
Dirty people being washed.
Captives being liberated.
Sinners becoming saints because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And once you understand that, something changes in the way you speak about somebody else's sexual brokenness.
You can still call sin sin.
But you cannot say it from a throne.
Because there is already Someone sitting there.
And it isn't you.

Perhaps that is what some Christians desperately need to remember before posting the next comment, sharing the next scandal, mocking the next fallen celebrity, attacking the next person whose sexuality they believe violates Scripture, or whispering about the next church member whose secret became public.
Truth does not become more biblical because you deliver it cruelly.
And compassion does not become more Christlike because you erase what God calls sin.
Jesus gives us something infinitely harder.
Truth without arrogance.
Grace without compromise.
Holiness without hatred.
Conviction without humiliation.
Love without lying.
Paul describes the posture beautifully in Galatians 6:1:
“καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος…”
Restore such a person “in a spirit of gentleness.”
That Greek verb, katartizete—καταρτίζετε—carries the idea of restoring, putting right, mending.
Think about that.
The goal is not destruction.
The goal is restoration.
When somebody has fallen, the mature Christian is not supposed to arrive like a spectator at a spiritual car crash.
We come carrying restoration.
And Paul immediately turns the mirror toward the person doing the restoring:
“σκοπῶν σεαυτόν…”
Watch yourself.
Why?
“lest you also be tempted.”

Galatians 6:1 does not permit indifference toward sin. It commands restoration. But it destroys the fantasy that the restorer stands above the fallen person as though temptation could never reach him.
The Christian approaches another sinner with truth in one hand and trembling humility in the other.
Because we know something about ourselves.
Given the right weakness...
the right loneliness...
the right opportunity...
the right secrecy...
the right unresolved wound...
the right moment of spiritual exhaustion...
we are not nearly as invincible as pride tells us we are.
That does not excuse sin.
It kills boasting.
There is a difference.

Romans 2 opens with another warning for the person who finds satisfaction in condemning others while overlooking his own rebellion. Paul warns that the one passing judgment can condemn himself while practicing the very things he denounces.
So biblical Christianity leaves no room for the smug Christian.
No room for the person saying, “Thank God I'm not like them.”
That sentence should sound familiar.
Jesus once told a story about two men praying.
One man's prayer was essentially a résumé.
He thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
The other could barely look upward.
He pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus said it was the broken man who went home justified.
That should terrify every Christian who has learned to use another person's sexual sin as evidence of his own righteousness.
Because you can have orthodox sexual ethics...
and a Pharisee's heart.
You can correctly define marriage...
and incorrectly represent Christ.
You can win an argument about sexuality...
while losing sight of the sinner standing in front of you.
You can quote Scripture accurately...
and secretly enjoy watching another human being bleed.
That isn't holiness.
That is pride wearing religious clothing.
But there is another ditch.
And Christians must refuse that one too.
Sometimes, because we are rightly horrified by self-righteousness, we become afraid to call anything sin.
We confuse kindness with silence.
We confuse compassion with affirmation.
We convince ourselves that loving someone means never telling them anything that could wound their feelings.
But Jesus did not die merely to make us comfortable with what is killing us.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly where you are.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ.”
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace does not merely remove condemnation; grace begins rebuilding the person who was condemned.
This is why the Gospel is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
It tells every one of us:
Your sin is worse than you wanted to admit.
And God's grace is greater than you dared to believe.
There is no sexual sinner beyond the reach of Christ.
Read that again.
No porn addict is beyond Christ.
No adulterer is beyond Christ.
No prostitute is beyond Christ.
No fornicator is beyond Christ.
No person with a sexually broken past is beyond Christ.
No person battling desires contrary to God's design is beyond Christ.
No person carrying memories they wish they could erase is beyond Christ.
And neither is the self-righteous Christian who has spent years hiding pride behind doctrine.
Jesus saves both.
This is where conversations about sexual sin must ultimately go.
Not merely toward “Stop.”
Toward Christ.
Not merely away from immorality.
Toward the One for whom our bodies were created.

Paul continues in 1 Corinthians 6 by declaring that the body is not for sexual immorality but for the Lord. He tells believers that their bodies belong to Christ and ultimately commands them to glorify God with their bodies.
Christian sexual ethics, then, are not fundamentally built upon disgust toward sexuality.
They are built upon belonging.
You belong to Christ.
Your body matters because Christ purchased you.
Your sexuality matters because Jesus is Lord over all of you.
Your desires do not outrank Him.
Neither do mine.
Your feelings do not become sovereign because they are powerful.
Neither do mine.
Your temptations do not define your identity.
Neither do mine.
The Christian confession is not, “Whatever I deeply desire must therefore be holy.”
It is:
“Jesus Christ is Lord.”
And sometimes surrender hurts.
Sometimes obedience costs something.
Sometimes repentance feels like a funeral because something we loved has to die.
But resurrection has always lived on the other side of death.
This is why Christians must be extremely careful about how we speak to people wrestling with sexual sin.
We are not speaking to categories.
We are speaking to souls.
That person you reduced to a label has a mother.
A childhood.
Memories.
Wounds.
Questions.
Nights when nobody knows they cried.
Maybe church people already wounded them.
Maybe Christians screamed at them but never listened to them.
Maybe somebody abused them and distorted their understanding of intimacy.
Maybe they know exactly what Scripture says and are exhausted from fighting desires nobody around them understands.
Maybe they are running from God.
Maybe they desperately want God.
Maybe they don't know what they believe anymore.
You do not know the entire story.
Jesus does.
So tell the truth.
But tell it like someone who knows what mercy tastes like.
Speak like someone who remembers the pit.
Speak like someone whose chains were broken by Another.
Speak like someone who understands that without Christ, your righteousness cannot save you either.
And when repentance happens...
do not keep introducing people by the chapter Jesus already redeemed.
Paul said:
“Such were some of you.”
Some Christians refuse to let people become “were.”
God forgives them, but we keep introducing them by their worst night.
“The adulterer.”
“The addict.”
“The promiscuous one.”
“The homosexual.”
“The woman who got pregnant.”
“The man who cheated.”
“The pastor who fell.”
“The girl with the past.”
But if genuine repentance and faith in Christ have taken place, the Gospel refuses to freeze a redeemed person inside the photograph of their greatest failure.
There is a reason Paul keeps saying:
But you were washed.
But you were sanctified.
But you were justified.
The Gospel has a but.
And sometimes one holy “but” changes an entire eternity.
You were guilty...
but Jesus.
You were enslaved...
but Jesus.
You were hiding...
but Jesus.
You thought your scandal had written the final sentence...
but Jesus.
This is why our message has never been “From Scandal to Respectability.”
It is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying a secret.
Maybe this article stopped being about “those people” several paragraphs ago.
Now it's you.
Your browser history.
Your affair.
Your lust.
Your hidden relationship.
Your fantasy life.
Your shame.
Your secret messages.
Your memories.
Your repeated promises to God.
“Lord, I'll never do it again.”
Then you did.
And now you are wondering whether Jesus is exhausted with you.
Listen carefully.
Do not turn grace into permission to remain enslaved.
But do not turn your repeated failure into proof that Christ cannot rescue you.
Run to Him.
Bring the ugly thing into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek accountability.
Cut off access where necessary.
Get help.
Tell a mature believer who will not flatter your sin or exploit your vulnerability.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
But run toward Jesus, not away from Him.
Your shame says, “Hide until you're clean.”
The Gospel says you cannot clean yourself enough to become your own savior.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness at the Cross.
There is cleansing.
There is power for transformation.
There is a new identity that does not have to be built around the thing that once mastered you.
And if you are the Christian reading this who has never struggled with that particular sin, there is a word for you too.
Stay humble.
You are not standing because you are better.
You stand by grace.
When someone falls, don't rush for a stone.
Reach for restoration.
The Christian who speaks about sexual holiness should sound like someone who has stood beneath a bloody Cross.
Because at Calvary nobody gets to brag.
There was only one innocent Man there.
And He was the One being crucified.
That changes everything.
It means we can look directly at sin without pretending it isn't sin.
And we can look directly at sinners without pretending they are beyond redemption.
It means we can preach repentance with tears in our eyes.
It means we can defend biblical marriage without despising people outside it.
It means we can warn without mocking.
Correct without crushing.
Disagree without dehumanizing.
Restore without pretending sin doesn't matter.
And love without rewriting God's Word to earn applause.
That is not weakness.
That is Gospel courage.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make one small confession of need.

And if Christ has genuinely rescued you from sexual brokenness, addiction, adultery, pornography, or another hidden bondage—and wisdom allows you to say so—leave a testimony that points to Jesus rather than yourself.
Someone reading silently may desperately need proof that repentance is not the end of the story.

Not because every sentence will feel comfortable, but because there may come a day when shame whispers that your failure is stronger than Christ's grace—or pride whispers that somebody else's failure makes you superior.
Come back and remember.
Nobody is saved by being less scandalous than his neighbor.
We are saved by Jesus Christ.
Not simply to help an algorithm.
Send it privately to the believer who needs encouragement.
That support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, encouraging, discipling, and placing Christ-centered resources before people who may never walk into a church building.
One Facebook share can carry the Gospel into a home we could never enter.
One tag can reach somebody we do not know.
One saved article can return to someone during the night they almost surrender to temptation.
And one person encountering Jesus through something you shared is worth infinitely more than impressive numbers on a screen.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
Come for Christ.
Stay close to His Word.
Support Gospel work freely if the Lord leads you and you are able.
And help carry the message to somebody else.
Because the world does not need Christians who pretend sexual sin isn't serious.
And it does not need Christians who behave as though sexual sinners are uniquely beyond grace.
It needs Christians who can stand beneath the Cross and say:
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
Jesus is Lord.
Grace is greater.
And transformation is possible.
So the next time someone's scandal becomes public, remember your own private need for mercy.
The next time someone confesses sexual sin, don't hand them permission to remain there.
But don't hand them a stone either.
Hand them the truth.
Point them toward repentance.
Walk with them toward restoration.
And above everything...
point them to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most Christlike thing we can say to a broken sinner is neither, “What you did doesn't matter,” nor, “What you did is all you will ever be.”
The Gospel says something far more powerful:
Your sin mattered enough that Christ had to die.
And His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to write your final chapter.
Never confuse the chapter where you fell with the ending Jesus is still writing.
